You have a continuous value at every cortical vertex--for example a *t*, *z*,
thickness, or connectivity map--and need a static figure that remains
scientifically interpretable after thresholding. The important distinction is
that the value is a **field on a triangle mesh**, not a parcel label. A polished
figure should therefore interpolate the scalar within each triangle, test
visibility with a real depth buffer, and add anatomy without drawing atlas or
occlusion lines over the result.

Two functions cover this task. `surface_figure()` renders both hemispheres
from several views and returns one finished figure with a shared colour bar;
`write_surface_figure()` writes it to PNG. Underneath it,
`render_surface_rgba()` is the deterministic, headless single-panel primitive:
it returns an RGBA raster plus diagnostic buffers and provenance, and
`write_surface_rgba()` writes one panel to PNG. Both run identically in CI,
on a cluster, and on a laptop, with no OpenGL and no browser.

## What are the inputs?

You need a display geometry and one numeric value per vertex. For anatomical
context, use sulcal depth or curvature from the same subject or template
rather than curvature computed on the inflated display shape. Sulci render
darker than gyri; the renderer detects whether a metric is larger in sulci
(as FreeSurfer `sulc` and `curv` are) and orients it accordingly.

The package bundles the fsaverage5 template (10,242 vertices per hemisphere)
with its sulcal depth, so this example runs offline.

```{r load-surfaces}
inflated <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "inflated")
white <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "white")
sulc <- load_fsaverage_sulc("fsaverage5")
```

Here smooth clusters stand in for your measured statistic. Each is placed at
a white-surface coordinate and falls off with distance measured over the
inflated surface, which follows the cortical sheet instead of cutting across
neighbouring sulcal banks. Widths differ between clusters and peaks differ
between hemispheres, as real effects do. The renderer treats the result like
any other vertex-wise numeric vector.

```{r make-statistic}
example_statistic <- function(hemi, side, peaks) {
  cluster <- function(centre, peak, width) {
    seed <- which.min(colSums((t(coords(white[[hemi]])) - centre)^2))
    xyz <- coords(inflated[[hemi]])
    peak * exp(-colSums((t(xyz) - xyz[seed, ])^2) / (2 * width^2))
  }
  # Inferior parietal, middle frontal, superior temporal and posterior
  # cingulate clusters
  cluster(c(45 * side, -60, 20), peaks[1], 12) +
    cluster(c(40 * side, 20, 30), peaks[2], 9) +
    cluster(c(55 * side, -20, 0), peaks[3], 8) +
    cluster(c(5 * side, -35, 25), peaks[4], 11)
}

stat_lh <- example_statistic("lh", -1, c(4, 3, -3.5, -3))
stat_rh <- example_statistic("rh", 1, c(3, 3.5, -2.5, -3.5))
```

The non-cortical medial wall should never carry statistical colour, so the
figures below also pass a cortex mask, one logical value per vertex. For a
subject, read it from FreeSurfer's `?h.cortex.label`. The bundled template
has no label file, so this example approximates one: across the medial wall
the fsaverage white and pial surfaces nearly coincide, so cortex is where
they are at least 1 mm apart.

A vertex-wise threshold leaves a stair-stepped boundary, so two rounds of
a majority vote over each vertex's neighbours smooth it.

```{r cortex-mask}
pial <- load_fsaverage("fsaverage5", "pial")
cortex <- lapply(c(lh = "lh", rh = "rh"), function(hemi) {
  gap <- coords(pial[[hemi]]) - coords(white[[hemi]])
  inside <- sqrt(rowSums(gap^2)) >= 1
  neighbours <- igraph::as_adjacency_matrix(graph(white[[hemi]]))
  for (i in 1:2) {
    votes <- as.vector(neighbours %*% inside)
    inside <- votes / Matrix::rowSums(neighbours) >= 0.5
  }
  inside
})
```

```{r validate-inputs, include=FALSE}
curv_lh <- sulc$lh
curv_rh <- sulc$rh
stopifnot(
  length(stat_lh) == length(curv_lh),
  length(stat_rh) == length(curv_rh),
  all(is.finite(stat_lh)),
  all(is.finite(stat_rh)),
  stats::sd(stat_lh) > 0,
  stats::sd(stat_rh) > 0
)
```

## How do you render one thresholded view?

Choose the threshold and colour limits as scientific inputs. In this example,
the colour scale stays fixed at `[-4, 4]`, while an opacity ramp softens
only the visual transition immediately above `|z| = 1.5`.

```{r render-one-view}
lh_lateral <- render_surface_rgba(
  inflated$lh,
  vertex_values = stat_lh,
  anatomy_metric = sulc$lh,
  cortex_mask = cortex$lh,
  camera = "lateral",
  threshold = 1.5,
  tail = "two_sided",
  limits = c(-4, 4),
  alpha_ramp = 0.25,
  antialias = 3
)
```

```{r validate-one-view, include=FALSE}
active <- as.integer(lh_lateral$overlay_alpha) > 0
stopifnot(
  any(lh_lateral$coverage),
  any(active),
  any(lh_lateral$coverage & !active),
  identical(lh_lateral$provenance$backend, "cpu_barycentric"),
  identical(lh_lateral$provenance$limits, c(-4, 4))
)
```

```{r show-one-view, echo=FALSE, out.width="80%", fig.align="center", fig.cap="Left hemisphere, lateral view. Two-sided *z*; |*z*| &lt; 1.5 is not drawn; colour limits &plusmn;4, blue negative, red positive. The four-view figure below carries the key."}
one_view_file <- knitr::fig_path("-cpu-lh-lateral.png")
dir.create(dirname(one_view_file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_surface_rgba(lh_lateral, one_view_file)
knitr::include_graphics(one_view_file)
```

The colour at each covered sample comes from the barycentrically interpolated
scalar. Thresholding and palette mapping happen after that interpolation, so a
threshold boundary may cross a triangle instead of jumping from one mesh edge
to the next. The per-sample z-buffer independently decides which folded surface
fragment is visible.

Surfaces are lit with interpolated normals, so cortical form reads without
drawn outlines, and the overlay keeps its colour-bar colour to within a few
percent at any viewing angle. Coarse meshes are subdivided for display
(`subdivide = "auto"`); the subdivision keeps every original vertex value and
never creates a suprathreshold region that linear interpolation would not.

## How do you build the four canonical views?

`surface_figure()` renders every hemisphere-view combination with one shared
threshold, colour limit, and palette, and adds the colour bar. The camera
contract is explicit: `camera_mode = "canonical"` is strict orthographic
output, while `"presentation"` adds a small declared obliquity.

```{r render-four-views}
figure <- surface_figure(
  lh = inflated$lh,
  rh = inflated$rh,
  values = list(lh = stat_lh, rh = stat_rh),
  anatomy = sulc,
  cortex_mask = cortex,
  views = c("lateral", "medial"),
  threshold = 1.5,
  tail = "two_sided",
  limits = c(-4, 4),
  alpha_ramp = 0.25,
  legend_title = "z",
  panel_width = 720,
  panel_height = 450,
  antialias = 3
)
```

```{r validate-four-views, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(
  length(figure$panels) == 4L,
  all(vapply(figure$panels, function(x) any(x$coverage), logical(1))),
  all(vapply(figure$panels, function(x) any(as.integer(x$overlay_alpha) > 0),
             logical(1)))
)
```

```{r show-four-views, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
figure_file <- knitr::fig_path("-cpu-four-views.png")
dir.create(dirname(figure_file), recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_surface_figure(figure, figure_file)
knitr::include_graphics(figure_file)
```

In an interactive session, `plot(figure)` draws the same figure on the
current graphics device.

The lateral and medial views differ because each panel rasterizes the visible
triangles from its own camera. Internal sulcal occlusion edges are not drawn as
outlines; `outer_contour = TRUE` marks only cortex touching background that is
connected to the image exterior.

## Where do the medial wall and cortex mask enter?

A real cortex mask is a separate domain object, not a consequence of parcel
value zero. Pass one logical value per vertex. Triangles touching a masked
vertex never receive overlay colour. `medial_wall` then controls whether the
excluded domain is quietly shaded, masked out, or outlined.

The panels below repeat the left medial view with each policy, using the
`cortex` mask from above. The posterior cingulate cluster runs up to the
wall; triangles that touch the wall receive no overlay colour under any
policy, so the cluster stops at the cortical boundary.

```{r cortex-mask-panels}
policies <- c("shade", "mask", "outline")
medial_panels <- lapply(policies, function(policy) {
  render_surface_rgba(
    inflated$lh, stat_lh, anatomy_metric = sulc$lh,
    camera = "medial", threshold = 1.5, limits = c(-4, 4),
    cortex_mask = cortex$lh, medial_wall = policy,
    width = 480, height = 300, antialias = 3
  )
})
```

```{r show-cortex-mask, echo=FALSE, fig.width=8, fig.height=1.9}
grid::grid.newpage()
layout <- grid::grid.layout(2, 3, heights = grid::unit(c(1, 1.4), c("null", "lines")))
grid::pushViewport(grid::viewport(layout = layout))
for (i in seq_along(medial_panels)) {
  panel <- medial_panels[[i]]
  raster <- grDevices::as.raster(
    array(as.numeric(panel$rgba) / 255, dim = dim(panel$rgba))
  )
  grid::grid.raster(raster, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1,
                                                layout.pos.col = i))
  grid::grid.text(
    sprintf('medial_wall = "%s"', c("shade", "mask", "outline")[i]),
    gp = grid::gpar(fontsize = 9, col = "#333333", fontfamily = "mono"),
    vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 2, layout.pos.col = i)
  )
}
```

Atlas-aware callers such as `neuroatlas::plot_brain()` can resolve the mask and
its provenance from an atlas annotation. At this low level, neurosurf requires
the caller to supply the domain explicitly rather than guessing that an atlas
label of zero always means medial wall.

## How should a volume become a continuous surface field?

For a continuous image, use explicit trilinear sampling through the cortical
ribbon. Interpolation, aggregation across depth, and tangential smoothing are
separate choices. The following call samples five depths, averages them, and
applies no surface smoothing. It needs your own subject's `white_surface`,
`pial_surface` and `statistic_volume`, so it is not run here:

```{r ribbon-projection, eval=FALSE}
mapped <- vol_to_surf(
  white_surface,
  pial_surface,
  statistic_volume,
  fun = "avg",
  sampling = "thickness",
  interpolation = "linear",
  depth = seq(0.1, 0.9, length.out = 5),
  aggregate = "mean",
  surface_smooth_fwhm = 0
)
```

Use `interpolation = "nearest"` for discrete nearest-voxel sampling. The
historical Gaussian KNN behaviour remains available as
`interpolation = "legacy"`. Categorical `aggregate = "mode"` is intentionally
incompatible with linear interpolation.

## Which function draws what you need?

Start from the output you want:

| You want | Use |
|---|---|
| A finished static figure: views by hemispheres, one colour bar | `surface_figure()`, then `write_surface_figure()` |
| One panel, or a custom layout you compose yourself | `render_surface_rgba()`, then `write_surface_rgba()` |
| To rotate and inspect a map on your desktop during analysis | `view_surface()` |
| An interactive figure in an HTML report or Shiny app | `surfwidget()`; see `vignette("interactive-surfaces")` |

The first two run headlessly and deterministically; the last two are
interactive sessions.

Two companion packages build on the same renderer, so their pixels agree with
the figures here: `neuroatlas::plot_brain()` adds atlas-derived masks, labels,
and orientation marks, and `neuromosaic::surf_montage()` starts from a
statistic volume rather than vertex values. Atlas outlines belong in figures
about the atlas; the default continuous-statistic view omits them.
